rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Hayyān rejects the Kufan parse of إلا ما يتلى عليكم as a nominative substitute: a badal cannot follow an affirmative clause, as in قام القوم إلا زيد.
rows.anchor: بعض الكوفيين من أنه في موضع رفع على البدل لا يصح البتة

rows.speaker: بعض الكوفيين
rows.claim: Some Kufans take إلا as a coordinator; Basran grammarians reject coordination here and allow an adjective for the preceding noun when it is indefinite or generic.
rows.anchor: وأما كون إلا عاطفة فهو شيء ذهب إليه بعض الكوفيين كما ذكر ابن عطية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says Ibn ʿAṭiyya may have conflated badal with adjective; unlike the adjective, badal does not require an indefinite or generic antecedent.
rows.anchor: فلعل ابن عطية اختلط عليه البدل والنعت ولم يفرق بينهما في الحكم

rows.speaker: الجمهور من المعربين والمفسرين
rows.claim: Most grammarians and exegetes parse غير محلي الصيد as a circumstantial accusative, and some claim consensus.
rows.anchor: واتفق جمهور من وقفنا على كلامه من المعربين والمفسرين على أنه منصوب على الحال

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash makes the implied subject of أوفوا the holder of the circumstantial phrase غير محلي الصيد.
rows.anchor: فقال الأخفش: هو ضمير الفاعل في أوفوا

rows.speaker: الجمهور والزمخشري وابن عطية وغيرهم
rows.claim: The majority, al-Zamakhsharī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and others make the pronoun in أحل لكم the holder of the circumstantial phrase.
rows.anchor: وقال الجمهور، والزمخشري، وابن عطية وغيرهما: هو الضمير المجرور في أحل لكم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some take the holder to be the omitted agent of the passive verb, identified as God.
rows.anchor: هو الفاعل المحذوف من أجل القائم مقامه المفعول به، وهو الله تعالى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another reported parse makes the pronoun in عليكم the holder of the circumstantial phrase.
rows.anchor: هو ضمير المجرور في عليكم

rows.speaker: البصريون (نقلا عن القرطبي)
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī reports a Basran analysis in which إلا ما يتلى عليكم and غير محلي الصيد are successive exceptions from بهيمة الأنعام.
rows.anchor: نقل القرطبي عن البصريين أن قوله: إلا ما يتلى عليكم، هو استثناء من بهيمة الأنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects that nested-exception reading as collapsing into permission to hunt during consecration; he also says Ibn ʿAṭiyya wrongly accuses others of confusion.
rows.anchor: وهذا وجه ساقط، فإذا معناه: أحلت لكم بهيمة الأنعام غير محلي الصيد وأنتم حرم إلا ما يتلى عليكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects al-Akhfash's parse: it separates the circumstantial phrase from its holder with a new ruling, wrongly restricts fulfillment of contracts, and yields awkward syntax if the game means wild animals.
rows.anchor: فأما قول الأخفش: ففيه الفصل بين ذي الحال والحال بجملة اعتراضية، بل هي منشئة أحكاما، وذلك لا يجوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects making the omitted agent of a passive verb the holder: such an agent is forgotten and cannot bear a circumstantial phrase, as in his المطر example.
rows.anchor: لأنهم نصوا على أن الفاعل المحذوف في مثل هذا التركيب يصير نسيا منسيا، ولا يجوز وقوع الحال منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive form is an original verbal form, not a transformed active form; moreover, that parse would make God’s permission of livestock conditional on not permitting hunting during ihram.
rows.anchor: لأن صيغة الفعل المبني للمفعول صيغة وضعت أصلا كما وضعت صيغته مبنيا للفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān locates the source of the parsing confusion in the yā spelling and readers' assumption that محلي is a plural active participle in construct with الصيد.
rows.anchor: وغرهم في ذلك كونه كتب محلي بالياء، وقدروه هم أنه اسم فاعل من أحل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān reads محلي الصيد like حسان النساء: محل describes the game, yielding the sense غير الصيد المحل, rather than describing people or an omitted agent.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: النساء الحسان، وكذلك هذا أصله غير الصيد المحل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He gives two senses of game being محل: it has entered the licit territory (al-ḥill), or God has made it lawful; game can be lawful or forbidden.
rows.anchor: ووصف الصيد بأنه محل على وجهين: أحدهما: أن يكون معناه دخل في الحل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ordinary Arabic ṣayd can name game without specifying lawful status, though in legal usage it is associated with lawful game.
rows.anchor: ولا يختص الصيد في لغة العرب بالحلال. ألا ترى إلى قول بعضهم: إنه ليصيد الأرانب حتى الثعالب

rows.speaker: شاعر غير مسمى
rows.claim: An unnamed poet's line uses يصطاد metaphorically of a lion hunting men, showing ṣayd can refer to prey beyond legally licit game.
rows.anchor: ليث بعثر يصطاد الرجال إذا ... ما كذب الليث عن أقرانه صدقا

rows.speaker: شاعر غير مسمى
rows.claim: An unnamed poet's line calls Salma a صيد caught by snares, another figurative use of hunting language.
rows.anchor: وقد ذهبت سلمى بعقلك كله ... فهل غير صيد أحرزته حبائله

rows.speaker: شاعر غير مسمى
rows.claim: An unnamed poet says Mayy catches men's hearts and lets Ibn ʿUmar and Ḥajar escape, further evidence for figurative ṣayd.
rows.anchor: ومي تصيد قلوب الرجال ... وأفلت منها ابن عمر وحجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the two exceptions cannot be nested without contradiction, if بهيمة الأنعام means livestock the exception is disconnected; if it includes wild game, it is connected under the interpretation that the game has entered al-ḥill while the pilgrims are consecrated.
rows.anchor: بل إن كان المعنى بقوله: بهيمة الأنعام، الأنعام أنفسها، فيكون استثناء منقطعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Game in the sanctuary is forbidden to both consecrated and nonconsecrated people, while game outside it is lawful to the latter; barring it from the consecrated is therefore a fortiori reason to bar sanctuary game.
rows.anchor: الصيد الذي في الحرم لا يحل للمحرم ولا لغير المحرم، وإنما يحل لغير المحرم الصيد الذي في الحل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ما يتلى عليكم refers to the bans that follow, its exception is disconnected because carrion and the other listed bans are not limited to wild animals; if the first noun includes livestock and game, the exceptions separately return to those two groups.
rows.anchor: إن كان المراد به ما جاء بعده من قوله: حرمت عليكم الميتة الآية، استثناء منقطعا

rows.speaker: النحويون
rows.claim: Grammarians say that when exceptions cannot be subtracted from one another, each exception applies to the original noun, as in the example listing Zayd, ʿAmr, and Bakr.
rows.anchor: وقد نص النحويون على أنه إذا لم يمكن استثناء بعض المستثنيات من بعض كانت كلها مستثنيات من الاسم الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The yā spelling and al-Farrāʾ's stopping at it do not disprove his parse: Qurʾānic orthography often differs from pronunciation, and one cannot pause between a construct noun and its complement.
rows.anchor: لا يعكر على هذا التخريج لأنهم كتبوا كثيرا رسم المصحف على ما يخالف النطق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says pausing on the yā was only for testing or because breath ran out, not a valid pause at the end of the construct noun.
rows.anchor: وأما وقفهم عليه بالياء فلا يجوز، لأنه لا يوقف على المضاف دون المضاف إليه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya praises the verse's eloquence and the abundance of meanings conveyed with few words.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية مما يلوح فصاحتها وكثرة معانيها على قلة ألفاظها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān responds with two lines from his poem praising the Messenger and the Qurʾān, composed in reply to Kaʿb's poem describing the Book.
rows.anchor: جار على منهج الأعراب أعجزهم ... باق مدى الدهر لا يأتيه تبديل

rows.speaker: رواية
rows.claim: A report says Surayḥ of Banū Ḍubayʿa went to Mecca as a pilgrim with sacrificial animals; in another version he carried trade goods, had spoken with the Prophet in Medina, and was suspected of conversion.
rows.anchor: خرج سريح أحد بني ضبيعة إلى مكة حاجا وساق الهدي

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet reportedly said of Surayḥ that he entered with a disbeliever's face and left with a traitor's heels.
rows.anchor: لقد دخل بوجه كافر وخرج بعقبي غادر

rows.speaker: رواية
rows.claim: In the Surayḥ report, he seized Medina's livestock, and its owners sought the Prophet's leave to raid him when he reached Mecca during al-Ḥudaybiyya; the verse was then revealed.
rows.anchor: فلما قدم مكة عام الحديبية أراد أهل السرح أن يغيروا عليه، واستأذنوا الرسول، فنزلت

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī names him al-Ḥuṭaym ibn Hind al-Baladī of Banū Ḍubayʿa and says the Prophet meant to send companions against him when the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: اسمه الحطيم بن هند البلدي أحد بني ضبيعة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the verse came at the conquest of Mecca, when Muslims proposed raiding polytheist pilgrims performing Hajj and ʿUmra.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: نزلت بمكة عام الفتح وحج المشركون واعتمروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shaʿāʾir is the plural of shaʿīra or shaʿāra, meaning God's marked limits, signs, and obedience; he had earlier explained it with the verse about Ṣafā and Marwa.
rows.anchor: والشعائر جمع شعيرة أو شعارة، أي: قد أشعر الله أنها حده وطاعته

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan takes the sacred signs to mean the whole religion, namely all the laws God has prescribed for His servants, so the phrase covers all divine obligations.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: دين الله كله يعني شرائعه التي حدها لعباده

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets God's signs here as the things forbidden during consecration.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: ما حرم عليكم في حال الإحرام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid identify the sacred signs as the rites of pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: وقال أيضا هو ومجاهد: مناسك الحج

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam enumerates six pilgrimage signs: Ṣafā and Marwa, sacrificial camels, the stone heaps, the Sacred Monument, ʿArafāt, and the Corner.
rows.anchor: شعائر الحج وهي ست: الصفا والمروة، والبدن، والجمار، والمشعر الحرام، وعرفة، والركن

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam also lists five sacred things: the Kaʿba, the sacred land, sacred month, Sacred Mosque, and the consecrated state until it ends.
rows.anchor: المحرمات خمس: الكعبة الحرام، والبلد الحرام، والشهر الحرام، والمسجد الحرام، حتى يحل

rows.speaker: ابن الكلبي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Kalbī says most Arabs did not count Ṣafā and Marwa among the sacred signs and Quraysh did not stand at ʿArafāt, so they were forbidden these practices.
rows.anchor: كان عامة العرب لا يعدون الصفا والمروة من الشعائر، وكانت قريش لا تقف بعرفات

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view identifies the signs as markers placed along the boundary between the licit territory and sanctuary, which people were forbidden to cross toward Mecca without consecration.
rows.anchor: الأعلام المنصوبة المتفرقة بين الحل والحرم نهوا أن يتجاوزوها إلى مكة بغير إحرام

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says the signs are offerings marked by blood from the hump or other tokens, citing 22:36; Abū Ḥayyān weakens this because the verse coordinates them with offerings and collars.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: هي الهدايا تطعن في سنامها وتقلد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān finds Abū ʿUbayda's interpretation weak because the verse separately mentions hady and collars after shaʿāʾir.
rows.anchor: وضعف قوله، بأنه قد عطف عليه. والهدي والقلائد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes shaʿāʾir to mean all things God has forbidden, whether during consecration or otherwise.
rows.anchor: هي ما حرم الله مطلقا سواء كان في الإحرام أو غيره

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī includes all ritual markers: pilgrimage stations and stone sites, circumambulation, and the rites of consecration, saʿy, shaving, and sacrifice.
rows.anchor: هي ما أشعر أي جعل إشعارا وعلما للنسك من مواقف الحج ومرامي الجمار

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī identifies the singular definite sacred month as the month of pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: فقال الزمخشري: هو شهر الحج

rows.speaker: عكرمة وقتادة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima and Qatāda identify the singular month as Dhū al-Qaʿda because it is the first sacred month.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة وقتادة: هو ذو القعدة من حيث كان أول الأشهر الحرم

rows.speaker: الطبري وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī and others identify it as Rajab, which is attributed to Muḍar.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري وغيره: رجب. ويضاف إلى مضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He explains the Rajab specification: Muḍar stopped fighting and laid weapons aside in that month; Arabs agreed on Dhū al-Qaʿda and Dhū al-Ḥijja but differed over Rajab, so God stressed it.
rows.anchor: وكانت العرب مجمعة على تعظيم ذي القعدة وذي الحجة، ومختلفة في رجب، فشدد تعالى أمره

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view reads الشهر as a generic singular, covering all four sacred months, and forbids fighting, raids, and looting in them.
rows.anchor: فالمراد به عموم الأشهر الحرم وهي: ذو القعدة، وذو الحجة، والمحرم، ورجب

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Mujātil says Junāda ibn ʿAwf would announce daily in the market of ʿUkāẓ that he had made one thing lawful and another forbidden.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: وكان جنادة بن عوف يقوم في سوق عكاظ كل يوم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says hady is livestock directed to the House as an offering, and God forbids people to seize or deem it lawful.
rows.anchor: لا خلاف أن الهدي ما هدي من النعم إلى بيت الله، وقصد به القربة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān notes that exegetes do disagree over the meaning of hady.
rows.anchor: والخلاف عن المفسرين فيه موجود

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view defines hady broadly as anything offered to God's House: camel, cow, sheep, charity, other sacrifices, or alms.
rows.anchor: هو اسم لما يهدى إلى بيت الله من ناقة أو بقرة أو شاة أو صدقة

rows.speaker: حديث
rows.claim: A hadith uses hady for even a chicken and then an egg, illustrating the broad lexical range of the word.
rows.anchor: في الحديث: ثم «كالمهدي دجاجة، ثم كالمهدي بيضة»

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says shaʿāʾir are the marked sacrificial camels, while hady includes cattle, sheep, garments, and anything given as an offering.
rows.anchor: الشعائر البدن من الأنعام، والهدي البقر والغنم والثياب وكل ما أهدي

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further distinction makes shaʿāʾir animals marked by bleeding the hump or other signs, and hady offerings identified by collars instead.
rows.anchor: الشعائر ما كان مشعرا بإسالة الدم من سنامه أو بغيره من العلائم، والهدي ما لم يشعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who understand shaʿāʾir as rites say hady is singled out as a specification of those rites.
rows.anchor: وقال من فسر الشعائر بالمناسك، ذكر الهدي تنبيها على تفصيلها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view describes hady as any offering made for God’s sake, and the source connects this usage with the hadith analogy of a chicken and an egg.
rows.anchor: هو ما قصد به وجه الله ومنه

rows.speaker: مجاهد وعطاء ومطرف بن الشخير
rows.claim: Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, and Muṭarrif ibn al-Shikhkhīr say collars were branches from sanctuary trees worn for safety; believers are forbidden this pre-Islamic custom and taking branches there.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد، وعطاء، ومطرف بن الشخير: القلائد هي ما كانوا يتقلدون به من شجر الحرم

rows.speaker: حديث
rows.claim: A hadith forbids cutting the sanctuary's fresh grass or trees.
rows.anchor: لا يختلى خلاها ولا يعضد شجرها

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most exegetes say pilgrims wore collars made from samur branches as a sign that they were on pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: القلائد ما كانوا يتقلدونه من السمر إذا خرجوا إلى الحج، فيكون ذلك علامة حجة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says a person from the sanctuary wore a collar when leaving for a need to show his sanctuary status, and the verse bars violating such a protected person.
rows.anchor: أو ما يقلده الحرمي إذا خرج لحاجة، ليدل ذلك على أنه حرمي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās that collars are the collared sacrificial offerings, while an offering is called hady before it is collared; thus both uncollared and collared offerings are named.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبري عن ابن عباس: أن القلائد هي الهدي المقلد، وأنه إنما سمي هديا ما لم يقلد

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects the claim that Ibn ʿAbbās limited hady to uncollared animals; he says the verse first forbids all offerings, then repeats collared ones for emphasis.
rows.anchor: وهذا تحامل على ألفاظ ابن عباس، وليس من كلامه أن الهدي، إنما يقال: لما لم يقلد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some take collars themselves as the object of the prohibition, a fortiori protecting the offerings they mark, as in the ban on displaying adornment that protects its locations.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أراد القلائد نفسها فنهى عن التعرض لقلائد الهدي مبالغة في النهي عن التعرض للهدي

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says the prohibition covers violating the sanctity of a collared offering or person; the collar stands for its bearer because the audience understood the reference.
rows.anchor: تأويله أنه نهى عن استحلال حرمة المقلد هديا كان أو إنسانا

rows.speaker: عبد الله وأصحابه
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh and his companions read آمي without the nūn of the construct phrase, meaning people headed to the Sacred Mosque, pilgrims and ʿumra visitors.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله وأصحابه: ولا آمي بحذف النون للإضافة إلى البيت

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains violating the signs as disregarding their sanctity, blocking worshippers, obstructing pilgrimage in its season, or stealing offerings or preventing them reaching their destination.
rows.anchor: وإحلال هذه أي: يتهاون بحرمة الشعائر، وأن يحال بينها وبين المتنسكين

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce يبتغون with yāʾ, making it an adjective of آمي.
rows.anchor: قرأ الجمهور يبتغون بالياء، فيكون صفة لآمين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī interprets فضل as reward; other interpreters take it as trade profits or increase in wealth and children.
rows.anchor: وفسر الزمخشري الفضل بالثواب، وهو قول بعضهم. وقيل: الفضل التجارة والأرباح فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking God's pleasure does not mean obtaining it; the pilgrims may seek it without receiving it.
rows.anchor: وأما الرضوان فإنهم كانوا يقصدونه وإن كانوا لا ينالونه، وابتغاء الشيء لا يدل على حصوله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view distributes the motives among polytheists: some sought trade without belief in an afterlife, while others sought divine pleasure through pilgrimage believing in resurrection, though they did not attain it.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو توزيع على المشركين، فمنهم من كان يبتغي التجارة إذ لا يعتقد معادا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says both Muslims and polytheists sought worldly benefit, while only believers sought God's pleasure.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كان المسلمون والمشركون يحجون، فابتغاء الفضل منهما، وابتغاء الرضوان من المؤمنين

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda interprets فضل and رضوان as God improving the pilgrims' worldly livelihoods and not hastening punishment for them in this life.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: هو أن يصلح معايشهم في الدنيا، ولا يعجل لهم العقوبة فيها

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say فضل and رضوان have one meaning: God's favor through mercy.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: الفضل والرضوان في الآية في معنى واحد وهو رضا الله تعالى وفضله بالرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition honors pilgrims of this description and protects them; it also wins over Arabs, encourages attendance at the pilgrimage season, lets them hear the Qurʾān and receive the proof, and may lead them to faith.
rows.anchor: وفي النهي عن التعرض لهم استئلاف للعرب ولطف بهم وتنشيط لورود الموسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the verse was revealed at the conquest, its rule for Muslim pilgrims remains operative while its rule concerning disbelievers was abrogated after year nine, when Abū Bakr led pilgrimage and al-Tawba was proclaimed.
rows.anchor: فكل ما كان فيها في حق مسلم حاج فهو محكم، أو في حق كافر فهو منسوخ

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو ميسرة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Abū Maysara say no part of the verse is abrogated; Abū Ḥayyān judges this view weak.
rows.anchor: وقول الحسن وأبي ميسرة: ليس فيها منسوخ، قول مرجوح

rows.speaker: حميد بن قيس والأعرج
rows.claim: Ḥumayd ibn Qays and al-Aʿraj read تبتغون in the second person, addressing believers who sought to fight and raid the polytheists in obedience to God's command and in pursuit of His pleasure.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حميد بن قيس والأعرج: تبتغون بالتاء خطابا للمؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that reading, the Muslims' purpose was God's command to fight polytheists, kill them, take captives and property, and continue until they believed or paid jizya.
rows.anchor: إذ أمر تعالى بقتال المشركين، وقتلهم وسبي ذراريهم، وأخذ أموالهم، حتى يؤمنوا أو يعطوا الجزية

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash reads رضوانا with ḍamma on rāʾ; Abū Ḥayyān notes this is also Abū Bakr's reading from ʿĀṣim in Āl ʿImrān, with a difference at the second occurrence in this sūra.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش: ورضوانا بضم الراء، وتقدم في آل عمران أنها قراءة أبي بكر عن عاصم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The permission to hunt after consecration returns to the earlier prohibition on hunting during ihram; the next ban on aggression reconnects to the command not to violate the pilgrims, an eloquent arrangement.
rows.anchor: وجاء ما بعدها من قوله: ولا يجرمنكم راجعا إلى الجملة الثانية، وهذا من بليغ الفصاحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hunting command establishes a ruling and is not a parenthetical interruption between the clauses about pilgrims and aggression.
rows.anchor: بل هي مؤسسة حكما لا مؤكدة مسددة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects an unnamed writer's proposal to rearrange the clauses and compare their order to the story of the cow, calling such postponement an ugly poetic necessity unsuitable to the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: وهذا لا يجوز عندنا إلا في ضرورة الشعر، وهو من أقبح الضرائر، فينبغي بل يجب أن ينزه القرآن عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the claim that Companions ordered the Qurʾān by thematic proximity rather than revelation order, holding that the Prophet arranged both its verses and sūras.
rows.anchor: بل الذي نعتقد أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم هو الذي رتبه لا الصحابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to hunt after the rites is permissive by consensus; hunting was originally lawful, and removal of the ihram restriction restores that default.
rows.anchor: والأمر بالاصطياد هنا أمر إباحة بالإجماع

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī paraphrases the command as saying there is no harm in hunting after release from consecration.
rows.anchor: ولهذا قال الزمخشري: وإذا حللتم فلا جناح عليكم أن تصطادوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He directs discussion of commands following prohibitions, and commands without contextual indicators, to legal theory.
rows.anchor: وتكلموا هنا على صيغة الأمر إذا جاءت بعد الحظر، وعليها إذا جاءت مجردة عن القرائن

rows.speaker: قراءة
rows.claim: A variant reads فإذا حللتم; حل and أحل are both Arabic forms meaning to come out of consecration.
rows.anchor: وقرئ: فإذا حللتم وهي لغة يقال: حل من إحرامه وأحل

rows.speaker: أبو واقد والجراح ونبيح والحسن بن عمران
rows.claim: Abū Wāqid, al-Jarrāḥ, Nabīḥ, and al-Ḥasan ibn ʿImrān read فاصطادوا with a kasra on its fāʾ; al-Zamakhsharī treats it as substituting for the initial hamza's kasra.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو واقد، والجراح، ونبيح، والحسن بن عمران: فاصطادوا بكسر الفاء

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the kasra reading difficult and suggests it recalls the kasra of hamzat al-waṣl when beginning the word.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: وهي قراءة مشكلة، ومن توجيهها أن يكون راعى كسر ألف الوصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says this is not pure kasra but imāla caused by imagining the kasra of the connecting hamza.
rows.anchor: وليس عندي كسرا محضا بل هو من باب الإمالة المحضة لتوهم وجود كسرة همزة الوصل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda gloss يجرمنكم as do not make you do something or carry you to it; this makes أن تعتدوا a phrase with an omitted preposition على.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس وقتادة: ولا يجرمنكم أي لا يحملنكم

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Others gloss the verb as earn or commit, with أن تعتدوا as its second object; the verb can also take one object, and Abū ʿAlī says it is best known for earning sins.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: معناها كسب التي تتعدى إلى اثنين، فيكون أن تعتدوا في موضع المفعول الثاني

rows.speaker: الحسن وإبراهيم وابن وثاب والوليد عن يعقوب
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Ibrāhīm, Ibn Waththāb, and al-Walīd from Yaʿqūb read يجرمنكم with a quiescent nūn, treating the emphatic nūn as light.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن، وإبراهيم. وابن وثاب، والوليد عن يعقوب: يجرمنكم بسكون النون

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains the phrase as resentment not causing or carrying the believers into aggression.
rows.anchor: لا يكسبنكم بغض قوم، لأن صدوكم الاعتداء، ولا يحملنكم عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says al-Zamakhsharī gives a semantic gloss, not a grammatical parse: the complement cannot simultaneously be a direct object of earning and follow carrying after an omitted preposition.
rows.anchor: وهذا تفسير معنى لا تفسير إعراب، لأنه يمتنع أن يكون مدلول حمل وكسب في استعمال واحد

rows.speaker: النحويان وابن كثير وحمزة وحفص ونافع
rows.claim: The two grammarians, Ibn Kathīr, Ḥamza, Ḥafṣ, and Nāfiʿ read شنآن with an open nūn; Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Bakr read it quiescent, also reported from Nāfiʿ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ النحويان وابن كثير، وحمزة، وحفص، ونافع: شنآن بفتح النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With open nūn, شنآن is most naturally a verbal noun on the common faʿlān pattern, though it can be an adjective on the less common pattern, meaning hating or hateful.
rows.anchor: والأظهر في الفتح أن يكون مصدرا، وقد كثر مجيء المصدر على فعلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As an adjective, شنآن means someone who hates and is transitive; as a verbal noun it can be annexed to its object, the more evident reading, or to its subject, meaning their hatred of you.
rows.anchor: ويعنون ببغيض مبغض اسم فاعل، لأنه من شنيء بمعنى البغض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With quiescent nūn, شنآن is most naturally an adjective; the forms شنآن/شنآنة are attested, and شنآن/شنأى imply an intransitive root, while roots can have both transitive and intransitive forms.
rows.anchor: والأظهر في السكون أن يكون وصفا، فقد حكي رجل شنآن وامرأة شنآنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A verbal-noun analysis with quiescent nūn is also possible, though that faʿlān verbal-noun pattern is rare; he cites ليانا and a line by al-Aḥwaṣ.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون مصدرا وقد حكى في مصادر شنيء، ومجيء المصدر على فعلان بفتح الفاء وسكون العين قليل

rows.speaker: الأحوص
rows.claim: Al-Aḥwaṣ's line uses الشنان for hatred; Abū Ḥayyān says it abbreviates شنآن by deleting the hamza and moving its vowel to the preceding consonant.
rows.anchor: وما الحب إلا ما تحب وتشتهي ... وإن لام فيه ذو الشنان وفندا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adjectival usage is more frequent than a verbal noun on this faʿlān pattern, as illustrated by رحمان.
rows.anchor: والوصف في فعلان أكثر من المصدر نحو رحمان

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وابن كثير
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Kathīr read إن صدوكم with kasra as a conditional; Ibn Masʿūd's إن صدوكم supports this reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو، وابن كثير: إن صدوكم بكسر الهمزة على أنها شرطية

rows.speaker: ابن جرير والنحاس وغيرهما
rows.claim: Ibn Jarīr, al-Naḥḥās, and others reject the conditional reading because the obstruction at al-Ḥudaybiyya occurred in year six before the verse's alleged revelation at the conquest in year eight, and Mecca was then under Muslim control.
rows.anchor: وأنكر ابن جرير والنحاس وغيرهما قراءة كسران، وقالوا: إنما صد المشركون الرسول والمؤمنون عام الحديبية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān strongly rejects their rejection: the reading is mutawātir among the seven and can mean that a similar obstruction occurs in future, for which the prohibition legislates.
rows.anchor: وهذا الإنكار منهم لهذه القراءة صعب جدا، فإنها قراءة متواترة، إذ هي في السبعة

rows.speaker: اليزيدي
rows.claim: The revelation date is not agreed: al-Yazīdī says the verse came before the obstruction, making the conditional reading straightforward.
rows.anchor: بل ذكر اليزيدي أنها نزلت قبل أن يصدوهم

rows.speaker: باقي السبعة
rows.claim: The other seven canonical readers open the hamza, making the phrase a causal explanation of resentment: they hated the people because they had obstructed them at al-Ḥudaybiyya.
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة: إن بفتح الهمزة جعلوه تعليلا للشنآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aggression here means retaliating against them by inflicting harm.
rows.anchor: والاعتداء الانتقام منهم بإلحاق المكروه بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After forbidding aggression, the verse positively commands mutual help in good and piety, since nonaggression alone still leaves neutral noncooperation as an option.
rows.anchor: لما نهى عن الاعتداء بأمر بالمساعدة والتظافر على الخير

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī glosses birr and taqwā as forgiveness and forbearance, while allowing the terms to cover every good and pious act, including forgiveness.
rows.anchor: وشرح الزمخشري البر والتقوى بالعفو والإغضاء

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say birr and taqwā are synonymous and repeated for emphasis; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this overindulgent, since customary usage covers required and recommended good while taqwā guards obligations.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: هما بمعنى واحد، وكرر لاختلاف اللفظ تأكيدا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says birr is what one is commanded to do and taqwā is what one is forbidden.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: البر ما ائتمرت به، والتقوى ما نهيت عنه

rows.speaker: سهل
rows.claim: Sahl says birr is faith and taqwā is the Sunna, meaning adherence to the prophetic practice.
rows.anchor: وقال سهل: البر الإيمان، والتقوى السنة. يعني: اتباع السنة
